summary: We simulate the crate minute by minute: find every fresh fruit touching a rotten one, then rot them all at once, and stop when a minute changes nothing (T10 — simulate until stable, with T8 grid neighbours). The key rule is "mark first, change later" so rot spreads only one step per minute.

blocks.title: Read the grid size from one line
blocks.text: `R` and `C` are typed on the SAME line (`3 3`), so we `split()` it and convert both parts with `map(int, …)`. Two separate `input()` calls would wait for a line that never comes.

blocks.title: Print the crate header
blocks.text: The sample shows the program printing `Enter the crate:` on its own line before the rows. Without this line the transcript does not match, even with the right answer.

blocks.title: Read the rows as lists of characters
blocks.text: Each row like `FFR` becomes `['F', 'F', 'R']`. We need lists because we change cells later, and Python strings cannot be changed in place. The rows have no prompt, so it is a plain `input()`.

blocks.title: Start a new minute
blocks.text: `minutes` counts the minutes in which something new rotted. Each pass of `while True` is one minute. `to_rot` only **collects** the fruits that will rot — if we changed the grid while scanning, a fruit that just rotted would spread again in the same minute.

blocks.title: Look at every fresh fruit
blocks.text: Two nested loops visit every cell; only a fresh `'F'` can become rotten, so the rest are skipped.

blocks.title: Does it touch a rotten fruit?
blocks.text: The four `(dr, dc)` pairs mean up, down, left and right. The bounds check `0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C` comes before `grid[nr][nc]`: without it, `nr = -1` reads the last row in Python. One rotten neighbour is enough, so we mark the fruit and `break` to avoid adding it twice.

blocks.title: Nothing new? Stop
blocks.text: If no fruit was marked, the crate is stable and this minute is **not** counted. This also handles a crate with no rotten fruit at all (answer 0).

blocks.title: Rot them all at once
blocks.text: Now every marked fruit turns `'R'` together, and we count the minute. Applying all changes after the scan is what makes them simultaneous.

complexity: At most R·C minutes, each scanning R·C cells × 4 neighbours; with a 10×10 grid that is ≤ 100 × 100 × 4 = 40,000 checks.
pitfalls: Changing cells during the scan → rot jumps several cells in one minute → answer too small.
No bounds check → `grid[-1]` silently reads the last row.
